source_title: herdr-core: terminals for coding agents - GitHub
source_excerpt:
hc runs programs and coding agents in terminals that stay alive after you leave. Agents can start other agents, send them work, and hear back; you can attach to any terminal and take over.
Core draws nothing. Use it from your shell, an agent, or your own app.
Builds are available for Linux and macOS on x86_64 and aarch64, and Windows on x86_64. Linux builds are static. On Windows, templates and quoted shell commands need sh on PATH, such as Git for Windows provides.
Run hc update to update. Running terminals keep running. See security for the trust and signing details.
Closing your viewer does not end the program. A waiting run checks in after 180 seconds by default, leaving the program running. It prints the terminal's address so you can read it or wait again.
For a terminal you want to keep even if its program is lost, use hc run --keep . Recovery starts a fresh shell, never reruns the task. A normal exit or an explicit kill still ends it.
With no program, hc run --bg starts the machine's shell: $SHELL (or /bin/sh ) on Unix, PowerShell 7 on Windows if available, else Windows PowerShell. Override it in ~/.config/herdr-core/config.toml (Windows: %APPDATA%\herdr-core\config.toml , or $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/herdr-core/config.toml when set):
The list is an executable followed by separate arguments, without extra path quoting. It must contain a nonempty executable. Changes apply to the next new shell or keep recovery, including recovery after a restart; no restart is needed. Running terminals, explicit programs, and quoted command lines keep their behavior. A bad setting reports a config error; a shell that cannot start reports spawn_failed . Recovery stays pending and retries, with errors in core.log (config) or holder.log (spawn); it never silently falls back to another shell.
Give an agent hc --skill . It prints the agent docs in one read, including how to delegate, wait, report back, and clean up.
Templates give an agent a command and a role. After saving the reviewer example from that page:
Agents started inside an hc terminal become its children. They can report back with hc send and wait for their children with hc wait --children all . The parent gets notes when a child needs attention or ends. Children end with their parent unless started with --outlive-parent .
Use the address returned by your run, not the example's box/t3 . Programs and files stay on that machine. Your local core brings its terminals into the same list. Machines covers SSH, custom connections, remote files, and reconnecting.
An agent can say it is working, done, blocked, or in error through OSC 7501, the Program Status Protocol. Core stores what it reports. It does not guess from screen text or recognize agent brands. A program that does not report status has none.
Use hc get review for a snapshot or hc events to follow changes.
hc schema prints the request/response API as OpenRPC with JSON Schema. The API docs cover connecting, terminal streams, events, and status. Use hc connect to carry the protocol over stdin and stdout, including through SSH.
Commands : generated from the binary's help.
Security : access, state, and updates.
For a quick lookup, run hc --help or a command's help, such as hc run --help . For agents, use hc --skill .
You need Rust, Zig 0.16, and just. CI pins the Rust version in .github/workflows/ci.yml .
just install installs this checkout and restarts your core. Running terminals keep running. just docs refreshes the command reference. just docs-check checks it and the examples; CI runs the same tests.
See CONTRIBUTING.md for contributor setup and checks.
License: Apache-2.0 . hc --licenses prints the included third-party licenses. After a dependency change, regenerate them with just notices .
